newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Bhutto's mother casts vote amid tight security.
newsitem.headline: Bhutto's mother casts vote amid tight security.

text.p: Nusrat Bhutto, the Iranian-born mother of ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto and a tragic figure in Pakistani politics, voted in Monday's election amid tight security.
Nusrat, a candidate for her daughter's Pakistan People's Party (PPP), is running against Ghinwa Bhutto, Lebanese-born widow of her son Murtaza, who was killed in September.
Ghinwa, 34, cast her vote in the same polling station earlier.
Nusrat, 67, officially designated "patron" of the PPP, has endured the pain of losing her husband and two sons, as well as the humiliation of seeing her daughter sacked twice as prime minister.

Her husband, former prime minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, was ousted by the military in 1977 and executed two years later. Her younger son, Shahnawaz, died of suspected poisoning in France in 1985. Murtaza was killed by police in Karachi on September 20.
Nusrat has remained in Benazir's entourage since Murtaza's unexplained killing. Benazir's husband, Asif Ali Zardari, is in jail on a charge of conspiring in his murder.
Zardari, backed by Benazir, says he is innocent.
A middle-aged woman led Nusrat by the hand into a polling station at a school-room in Larkana, home town of the Bhutto clan in the southern province of Sindh.
She stamped national and provincial assembly ballot papers on Nusrat's behalf, but did not show her identity card as required. "We'll send the card later," she snapped.
"Everybody knows Begum Sahiba (Nusrat)," said an electoral officer when asked why she had issued the ballot papers without seeing Nusrat's identity card or taking her thumb print.
"It is not rigging," she said, explaining that Nusrat had forgotten to bring her card.
Ghinwa, leading the splinter PPP-Shaheed Bhutto party set up by her husband, has said she has been unable to contact Nusrat, who is reported to be suffering from Alzheimer's Disease.
"I am fine," said Nusrat with a glassy smile, when reporters at the polling station inquired about her health.
Nusrat's women companions pulled her away when she was asked if Benazir was holding her hostage. "Keep away, keep away," one of the minders warned, as soldiers and policemen stood by.
Ghinwa's supporters say Benazir effectively kidnapped her mother after Murtaza's death and controls her movements. PPP leaders dismiss as absurd the notion that Nusrat is a hostage.

President Farooq Leghari, a former PPP secretary general, ordered Monday's elections after sacking Benazir's government on November 5 on disputed charges of corruption and misrule -- the second time Benazir had been sacked by a president in six years.
Last week the Supreme Court ruled that there was enough evidence of corruption, nepotism and other abuses to justify Leghari's action and rejected Benazir's plea for reinstatement.
